label: Final Comments
notes: Open the closing chapter. Having built the theory from conics to cubic surfaces, we step back and look forward. The deck follows printed pages 121 through 132 and surveys where the subject goes next: schemes, sheaves and cohomology, the role of the field, and the threads connecting the explicit geometry we studied to the modern abstract framework.

label: From Varieties to Schemes
notes: Point toward schemes, the modern generalization of varieties due to Grothendieck. By allowing arbitrary commutative rings and nilpotent elements, schemes handle non-reduced structure, families, and arithmetic uniformly. The affine variety theory we developed is exactly the reduced, finite-type case over a field, the doorway into this far broader landscape.

label: Sheaves and Cohomology
notes: Preview sheaves and their cohomology, the tools that make local-to-global reasoning systematic. Cohomology groups measure obstructions, count sections, and power theorems like Riemann-Roch. They turn the bookkeeping of functions and forms on a variety into computable linear algebra and are indispensable in every part of modern algebraic geometry.

label: The Role of the Field
notes: Reflect on the base field. Working over an algebraically closed field gave the cleanest statements, but the same equations over the rationals or finite fields carry deep arithmetic, from Diophantine problems to the Weil conjectures. Algebraic geometry over different fields is the meeting point of geometry, number theory, and arithmetic.

label: Where the Subject Goes
notes: Survey the roads ahead: curves and their Jacobians, the classification of surfaces, moduli spaces parametrizing geometric objects, intersection theory, and connections to physics and coding theory. Each grows directly from the concrete examples in this book, showing how the playful study of curves opens onto a vast and active discipline.

label: Recap
notes: Close the course. We began by playing with conics and cubics, built the precise dictionary of affine varieties, added projective and birational tools, and counted the lines on a cubic surface. Schemes, sheaves, cohomology, and arithmetic over varied fields are the natural continuations, and the explicit habits learned here remain the surest guide into them.
